newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong fireworks team battles the elements.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong fireworks team battles the elements.

text.p: Rain is the enemy as two dozen British and Chinese workers scramble to ready 27 tonnes of fireworks for an extravanganza on the evening Hong Kong reverts to Beijing rule.

A red explosives flag flies over the three fireworks barges which are pitching in rough water at the Dangerous Goods Anchorage on the western approach to Hong Kong harbour, a place where nuclear submarines and ships carrying hazardous chemicals also are held.
Signs warning "No Smoking" and "No Open Light" are posted prominently on the barges, where men are carefully packing paper-wrapped explosive charges down fibreglass mortar tubes.

Hong Kong's soaring office towers are barely visible to the southeast, obscured by a seasonal rain storm moving across the harbour towards the barges. Thunder rumbles as occasional bolts of lightning split the sky.
"Well, the lightning makes it a bit more exciting, I'll give you that," said Mark Lancaster of Kimbolton Fireworks, one of two companies responsible for manufacturing and producing the fireworks.
"Lightning is always a worry but these are flat barges and there are a lot of taller things in the harbour so we should be OK."
If all goes well on June 30 the three barges will be towed to a point in the harbour just off the site of the handover ceremony.
Then, precisely at 8.15 p.m., just three and a quarter hours before Hong Kong passes from Britain back to China, the first salvo in a gala 20-minute firework display will explode over the harbour.
More than half a million people are expected to view the fireworks in person and as many as 100 million others could see it on television.
Nearly 20,000 separate explosions have been programmed -- half of them supplied by the British firm Kimbolton and the other half by Sunny Fireworks, a Chinese firm from Guangzhou.
"I think this has to be one of the best places in the world for fireworks in terms of backdrop, but the weather could be a problem," Lancaster told reporters on Thursday.
"We're losing time (because of rainy weather) but we should be OK. It (rain) only affects the setting up, not the firing."

Once the firing tubes have been loaded and the fuses set the fireworks are covered in plastic. If necessary they can be fired directly through the plastic, so once they are set up the weather is less of a worry.
Rain on handover day would be one thing but a typhoon would be something else entirely, admitted Edward Naylor, head of Corporate Affairs for ING Barings, sole sponsor of the June 30 fireworks.
"If there's a typhoon it's off and that's that, presumably," Naylor said. "I doubt it could be rescheduled for later."
The June 30 fireworks will cost Barings $HK3.9 million ($US500,000). An even larger and more expensive fireworks display is set for Hong Kong harbour on the evening of July 1.
